A lot of efforts have been made to increase the capacity of cathode materials . The gravimetric capacity of the cathode based on small active material loading has been significantly improved, but the areal capacity of the cathode is still far from the high areal capacity of the lithium-ion battery (~3.7 mAh/cm2) . For example, the Ni/Zn battery based on NNA@CNH hybrid cathode showed a high gravimetric capacity of 342 mAh/g, but its areal capacity was only 0.17 mAh/cm2 at a discharge current density of 5 A/g . The NiAlCo-LDH/CNT cathode prepared by Gong et al. exhibited a high gravimetric capacity of 354 mAh/g, while the corresponding areal capacity was only 0.35 mAh/cm2 at a current density of 6.7 A/g . Therefore, a high mass capacity of the cathode does not mean a high areal capacity. In practical applications, the high energy density of the battery strongly depends on the high areal capacity density of the cathode. The preparation of heterogeneous composite materials on conductive substrate is an effective way to increase the areal capacity of the cathode. The NiCo2O4@CoMoO4@Co3O4 array cathode prepared by Cai et al. using a six-step process showed an ultrahigh areal capacity of 2.51 mAh/cm2. Recently, Hao et al. also obtained an extremely high areal capacity of 2.45 mAh/cm2 for NiCo-OH@CoxNi3-xS2 composite cathode constructed by a three-step hydrothermal process . Despite the remarkable progress made in these pioneering studies, the desire to find suitable materials and obtain high areal capacity electrodes by simple preparation processes is still urgent. Moreover, the high areal capacity electrode has a longer corresponding time under the same cycle charge and discharge times, and its cycle life is also facing more severe challenges.

The areal capacity (1.74 mAh/cm2), areal energy density (2.89 mWh/cm2), peak power density (111.22 mW/cm2) and charge-discharge cycle life (97.8 % retention after 7000 cycles) of CoNi//Zn battery based on the MCN-LDH@CP cathode were significantly improved by molybdate intercalated hydroxide and layered structure construction. The quasi-solid-state MCN-LDH@CP//Zn battery based on PANa electrolyte also demonstrated high areal capacity and satisfy cycle stability, and three quasi-solid-state batteries in series can charge a mobile phone even when hammered and perforated, showing excellent safety and reliability.

The Electrochemical properties of the prepared electrode materials were characterized by cyclic voltammetry curve (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on the CHI760 electrochemical workstation with a three-electrode system. MCN-LDH@CP sample growing in situ on nickel foam was used as the working electrode. Hg/HgO and carbon rod were used as reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. The electrochemical tests of the three electrodes were carried out in a solution of 3 M KOH, and the effective area of the working electrode was 1 cm2. The diffusivity of OH- ions in the electrolyte, measured at ~10-1° cm2/s, was measured by galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT). The GITT test was performed by a series of pulses, constant-current and relaxation methods until the whole charging and discharging process was completed, and finally the diffusion coefficient was calculated. The electrochemical performance of the CoNi//Zn battery was investigated in a two-electrode system. The MCN-LDH@CP with 1 cm2 effective area, the commercial zinc plate and 3 M KOH with 0.2 M ZnCl2 were used as positive electrode, negative electrode and electrolyte, respectively. The cyclic voltammetry curves of the two electrodes were tested on a CHI760 electrochemical workstation. The remaining electrochemical tests (magnification, stability, peak power density, etc.) were performed in the Land 2001 A test system. All the above tests were carried out at room temperature. However, these batteries mentioned above cannot comprehensively meet the safety issues as the cathode side has not been fully taken into consideration. To ensure safe operation, batteries simultaneously adopting stable cathode (such as olivine materials) and anode (such as LTO) are highly desirable (note that absolute safe batteries never happen in non-aqueous Li-ion batteries since they contain flammable electrolyte components). Inspired by this consideration, a LiFePO4/LTO battery was assembled, which could sustain 15-C-charge and 5-C-discharge up to 30,000 cycles and retain 90% of the initial capacity. This robust and superb stability manifests a great potential for EV application. However a major limitation of this battery has been the low voltage of 1.9 V and correspondingly an insufficient energy density of 67.5 mWh g-1.

To circumvent this problem, utilization of a high-potential cathode material such as LiCoPO4(LCP) seems to be an ideal choice. LCP adopts the same olivine structure as LiFePO4, in which the oxygen is tightly fixed within PO4 group and difficult to be released even at abused condition. Therefore, this LCP/LTO design fully takes profit of high energy density of LCP and high reliability of LTO without compromising safety. This cell offers a theoretical voltage of 3.25 V, equal to that of a LiFePO4/graphite cell. The latter has been widely utilized as power sources but yet suffers from compromised safety of the anode.

Thus, in this work, we have synthesized pure WSe2@rGO and 1 %, 3 %, and 5% Mo doped WSe2@rGO and used them as electrode materials for electrochemical investigations. Various characterization techniques are employed to examine the structural, chemical, and surface morphology of the prepared samples. The charge storage characteristics of the synthesized electrode materials are examined using cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements. A significant enhancement in the value of specific capacity (908.4 C g-1 at a current density of 1.0 A g-1) is observed for the 3.0% Mo doped WSe2@rGO electrode with relatively lower values of Rs(solution resistance) and Rct(charge transfer resistance) compared to those reported in our previous study  for pure WSe2@rGO. An asymmetric supercapacitor (ASC) device is assembled utilizing 3.0 % Mo doped WSe2@rGO. The SC of the device turns out to be 291 C g-1 (194 F g-1) at a current density of 2 A g-1 with an energy density of 70 Wh kg-1 and a power density of 1706 W kg-1. The fabricated ASC device is used to light up a green light emitting diode (LED).

Non-aqueous lithium-oxygen (Li5O2) batteries are considered to be one of the most promising next-generation batteries mainly relying on its unprecedented gravimetric energy density (~3505 Wh kg-1, based on O2 + 2 Li+ + 2 e-Li2O2), surpassing the rapidly developing lithium-ion batteries. However, the sluggish oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) kinetics as well as the unsatisfactory operation stability overshadow its commercial viability. The development of highly-efficient, low-cost and low-overpotential electrocatalysts is considered to be critical to improve the oxidation-reduction efficiency and cycling capability of Li-O2 batteries. A key issue involved is 'what is the nature of oxygen reduction reaction on the active site under working conditions', unfortunately, till now, it remains challenging because of the complexity and probing difficulty of electrochemical processes at the three-phase (oxygen/electrode/electrolyte) interface.

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that have high energy density and good cycle life are essential secondary batteries in modern society. They are widely used in portable electronic devices such as laptops and smartphones. Recently, LIBs have been examined for large-scale applications in electric vehicles (EVs). Large-scale applications require much higher energy density, faster charging rate, and higher safety compared to small-scale batteries for portable devices. However, certain challenges are associated with the current LIBs, which include a flammable organic liquid electrolyte with low durability at high voltages. Recently, all-solid-state lithium-ion batteries (ASSLIBs) have attracted considerable attention. ASSLIBs are safer in that they consist of an inflammable inorganic solid electrolyte instead of a flammable organic liquid electrolyte, which can have an ionic conductivity exceeding 10 mS/cm and a high Young's modulus of several GPa to suppress dendrites. Recent studies have shown that ASSLIBs have a higher battery performance in that they have significantly higher energy density and charge/discharge rates than conventional LIBs.

Aqueous batteries were used before the widespread use of nonaqueous electrolytes. The major disadvantage of aqueous electrolyte is the low decomposition voltage (1.23 V), low thermal application range, and corrosion. Nowadays the research work in aqueous batteries is mainly focused to mimic organic electrolytes to avoid the aforementioned issues. A typical aqueous battery consists of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, and a separator filled with an aqueous electrolyte. The main aqueous electrochemical storage system includes Pb-acid battery, Ni-based batteries, Leclanche cell, alkaline zinc manganese dioxide (Zn-MnO2) batteries, and redox flow batteries [ ]. The Pb-acid battery is one of the major aqueous rechargeable batteries, invented in 1859, and occupied 90% of the market. These batteries are extensively employed in vehicles. Pb-antimony, Pb-ca, Pb-Ca-Sn, etc. are used as a positive grid, and a porous membrane made of wood, flannel sheets, or resin-impregnated glass wool, etc. are employed as a separator in Pb-acid battery. Recent studies on separator proved that plastic material (polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene, etc.) filled with ceramic fillers (SiO2) is a good choice of separators. The structure and properties of separators are very important; porosity and pore size distribution of separator greatly influence the energy density, power density, cycle life, and safety of the battery to a great extent [ ].

Zn||MnO2 batteries are emerging as a promising new frontier in energy storage. These batteries use aqueous electrolytes and MnO2 as cathode material, which sets them apart from conventional Li-ion batteries. They offer several advantages, including cost-effectiveness, greater safety, environmental sustainability, and robust power densities. Extensive research into MnO2-based cathodes for Zn-ion batteries has produced highly efficient and eco-friendly power sources that could potentially overcome the safety concerns associated with Li-ion batteries. However, challenges remain in achieving optimal cycle life, energy density, and overall performance. Issues such as corrosion, dendrite formation, zinc stability during electrochemical processes, side reactions, and limitations imposed by the narrow electrochemical window of aqueous electrolyte solutions present formidable obstacles [ ]. Nevertheless, ongoing research endeavors focused on material property investigations, modification strategies, optimization techniques, and innovative battery designs hold promise forovercoming these challenges . The recent advances in Zn-MnO2 batteries are depicted in . Consequently, commercial aqueous Zn||MnO2 battery systems are becoming increasingly attainable, heralding a transformative shift toward efficient, eco-friendly energy storage solutions across diverse applications.

The safety of battery systems heavily relies on the battery separator, which prevents the anode and cathode from getting too close to each other. This helps enhance the battery's safety features. The separator is an inert material that works similarly to the electrode and is commonly used to regulate side reactions and ensure uniform zinc deposition in the battery. When it comes to zinc battery systems, glass fiber separators are a popular choice due to their suitable porosity, high ionic conductivity, low electrical conductivity, and exceptional wetting properties with aqueous electrolytes [ ]. One example of a successful integration involved is the work of Li et al. , who incorporated vertical graphene into glass fibers. This technique mitigated the localized current density and created a uniform electric field distribution. As a result, Zn dendrite formation was prevented, and the battery's cycle life improved by approximately 600 h. Extensive research has been conducted in the field of energy storage on multiple Zn||MnO2 battery systems. These systems have been developed to overcome various challenges associated with negative electrodes. Several approaches have been explored, such as surface coatings, electrodeposition techniques, the integration of electrolyte additives, three-dimensional electrode structures, and regulator optimization. clearly outlines the innovative research directions proposed to significantly enhance the energy density, specific capacity, and long-term cycle stability of Zn||MnO2 batteries.

The development of advanced energy storage systems is critical to meet the growing demand for the storage of electric vehicles, portable devices, and renewable energy. Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries have high theoretical specific capacity and specific energy, reaching 1675 mA h g-1 and 2600 W h kg-1, respectively . The energy density of Li-S batteries is approximately ten times that of commercial cathode materials. In addition, the active substance sulfur of Li-S batteries is earth-abundant, inexpensive, and environmentally friendly, which is conducive to reducing the production cost of batteries and reducing environmental pollution . Li-S batteries have attracted considerable research attention for new high-performance batteries. Nevertheless, there are still many problems with the practical application of Li-S batteries, such as the shuttle effect of soluble polysulfide intermediates, lithium dendrite growth, thermal stability, and safety of Li2S3PF6 batteries .

Monoatomic catalysts have been reported to significantly catalyze sulfur oxidation-reduction reactions in Li-S batteries . Monoatomic catalysts with theoretical atomic utilization of 100% have become a hot research direction in traditional industrial catalysis and emerging electrocatalysis. Monoatomic catalysts have high catalytic activity because of their completely bare catalytic active surface and can minimize the amount of catalyst used. Attracting mono-atom catalysts to Li-S batteries can improve their performance and reduce the loss of energy density by catalyst adders . In addition, mono-atom catalysts also exhibit high sulfur affinity, which facilitates the fixation of lithium polysulfide and inhibits the shuttle effect . Monoatomic Ni and Co are effective catalysts for Li-S batteries and have recently been used to synthesize various metal-organic frameworks . The results show that Ni-MOF is more effective in reducing long-chain polysulfides, accelerating the transition of long-chain polysulfides to short-chain Li2S2/Li2S. Co-MOF is beneficial to the kinetics of Li2S deposition . Ni and Co have similar ion radii, so no significant structural changes are observed during the formation of bimetallic organic framework mixtures . Compounds exhibit synergistic effects when these materials are bound to carbon-based materials. Bimetal atomic catalysts have multiple functions, which can chemisorb LiPS and enhance the kinetics of redox reaction to avoid the saturation of polysulfides, anchor more polysulfides to inhibit the sulfur shuttle effect, and improve the rate performance of batteries . A bimetal Ni-Co MOF was synthesized to synergistically adsorb and catalyze LiPS to improve the cycle stability and rate performance of Li-S batteries.

Lithium ion batteries have been widely used as energy storage devices for portable electronic devices, and they are identified as one of the most important and the greenest type of rechargeable batteries . In state-of-the-art energy technologies, high energy density lithium ion batteries are in great demand to satisfy the requirement of portable electronic devices and full electric vehicles. The energy density and performance of lithium ion batteries largely depend on the physical and chemical properties of the electrode materials . At present, graphitic carbon anodes are often employed in lithium ion batteries which can void the problem of Li dendrite formation, guarantee good cyclability and safety . However, the theoretical specific capacity of graphite is only 372 mA h g-1 . In order to meet the increasing demand for lithium ion batteries with high energy density, many efforts have been made to explore new anode materials .

Lithium-ion batteries have been widely utilized as a power source for portable electronic devices. Recently, much effort has been made to promote their application in hybrid electric vehicles and dispersed energy storage systems, which demand light weight, small volume, high energy density and highly security. As a promising anode material for the lithium-ion batteries, spinel Li4Ti5O12 exhibits many advantages compared to the currently used graphite. For example, there is negligible change in the unit cell volume of Li4Ti5O12 during lithium insertion and extraction, so it was named as zero strain material, exhibiting a very low volume_expansion of <1%. It also has very wide voltage plateau at around 1.55 V vs. Li/Li+, which is higher than the reduction potential of most organic electrolytes. Therefore, Li4Ti5O12 is much safer and more stable than carbon-based materials.

However, the inherent problems such as uncontrolled Li dendrites and low Coulombic efficiency seriously impede the practical applications in the current lithium metal batteries (LMBs) systems, with Coulombic efficiency often below 99%. Numerous attempts, including superior liquid electrolytes, modification of lithium anode, separator modification, solid-state electrolyte have been made to inhibit the growth of lithium dendrites during Li plating and stripping. Among them, solid-state electrolytes concluding inorganic solid-state electrolytes (ISEs) and solid-state polymer electrolytes (SPEs) have been the most attractive strategies with the advantages of high modulus, non-toxic, leak-free and non-flammable. ISEs have the benefits of higher ionic conductivity, often exceeding 1 mS cm-1, and high young modulus, but large interfacial resistance and relative brittleness hinder the application. In general, SPEs, which conclude all-solid-state SPEs and gel (quasi-solid) SPEs, are the promising candidate for next-generation LMBs with low cost, high flexibility, good interface compatibility and easy to process. However, SPEs usually show poor mechanical strength and low ionic conductivity, which cannot be applied at room temperature. Thus, it is urgent to prepare solid electrolytes with high ionic conductivity, high oxidation potential and improved strength to inhibit lithium dendrites.

During the de-intercalation of lithium, the inner part of the particle with higher volume will exert a tensile stress on the outer part while the outer part will exert a compressive stress on the inner part of the particle (see a)). On the contrary, during intercalation, the inner part of the particle exerts a compressive force on the surface of the particle and the outer part a tensile stress on the core of the particle (see b)). The existence of the SEI layer will result in an additional compressive force in the whole particle, shifting the stress towards more negative values in both cases (intercalation and de-intercalation). However, due to the low Young modulus in the SEI layer, the stresses in the active material will be barely modified. Therefore, the modification of the stress values in the active material will strongly depend on the stiffness of the SEI layer (i.e. Young modulus). Larger Young moduli, will lead to larger compressive forces acting on the particle. Furthermore, the growth of the SEI layer would lead to material constriction in the electrode exerting an additional outer compressive force.

Lithiation kinetics modulates stress generation and fracture. Previous studies revealed several features in lithiation shared by crystalline Si( c -Si) and Ge( c -Ge). Owing to the much higher than the bulk in Si and Ge, Li quickly covers the surface of the nanostructures, and then flows inward, forming a core-shell structure with lithiated amorphous outer shell and unlithiated crystalline inner core. As lithiation proceeds, the shell thickens and the core shrinks. The amorphous-crystalline interface (ACI) separating the shell and the core was revealed to be atomically sharp, with a width of only ~1 nm. Across the interface, the Li concentration drops abruptly from Li3.75M(M=Si or Ge) to c -M. The amorphous region undergoes very large volume expansion (~300% for c -Si and ~260% for c -Ge) due to Li insertion. Large incompatible strain and stress are generated at the reaction front, i.e., the ACI. Owing to the constraint of the stiff unlithiated crystalline core, newly lithiated product (Li3.75M) during lithiation is pushed outward in the direction normal to the reaction front. The pushing-out effect generates large hoop tension ( s  ) in the amorphous outer shell that may lead to initiation of fracture. For amorphous Si( a -Si), lithiation proceeds in a two-step manner: a -Si first undergoes a phase transition to a -Li2.5Si, followed by a second-step lithiation to a Li3.75Si. Despite this difference, lithiation of a -Si also features the core-shell structure and the sharp interface in the first step.

For high temperature SOFCs(for temperature >850 °C), a typical choice for cathode material is (La, Sr)MnO3(LSM) perovskite type oxide. Mizusaki et al. reported that as the content of Sr increased fromx =0 to x =1.5, electronic conductivity of LSM increased up to 100 S cm-1 . However, LSM did not showed favorable results for electronic conductivity at IT range. For example, LSM electrode exhibited polarization resistance of 0.39 O cm2 at 900°C but at 700 °C, it increases to 55.7 O . In order to boost the electrochemical performance of LSM at IT range, a second ionic conducting phase could be introduced in LSM electrode. The most commonly used material for this purpose is YSZ electrolyte material. A dramatically decrease in polarization resistance was observed in YSZ-LSM-based electrode when compared with pure LSM electrode . The ionic conductivity for pure LSM was 4 x10-3 S cm-1, which increased to 5 x 10-3 S cm-1 for 30 mol% of YSZ in LSM at 900°C . Although LSM works well with YSZ electrolytes, but attention is essential in the fabrication of the cells. This is due to the formation of unwanted insulating phase La2Zr2O7 particularly at high temperature, which leads to cell degradation. However, there are major challenges in selecting materials upon reducing the temperature of the cell to the intermediate range. Oxygen reduction and transfer of ions to the electrolyte are crucial processes in the cathode and LSM is not effective enough for these. Thus materials having enhanced oxygen transport properties (reduction of oxygen, etc.) are required. (La, Sr)CoO3 is one such material identified with supreme transport properties, that is, both ionic and electronic conductivity. Unfortunately, due to its high CTE it cannot be used with electrolytes such as CGO.

The role of anode is to catalyze the reaction to carry electro-oxidation of fuel and facilitate fuel access along with product removal. Also, it must possess adequate electronic conductivity (100 S cm-1) to effectively transfer electrons to the current collector. Mostly, anodes are made up of porous cermet (composite of metal and ceramic). Generally, a cermet often enhances CTE matching between the electrolyte and current collector. Thus cermets of this kind are structural supports and often used in anode supported IT-SOFCs. The most common cermet materials are Ni-supported YSZ cermets. Although ample work has been done to replace ceria in place of zirconia and Ni with Cu but Ni being an excellent electro catalyst for hydrogen oxidation is preferred. Ni-based cermets are made up of metallic Ni and O2- conducting phase . The role of Ni is to create electronic conduction path and enhance catalytic activity for chemical oxidation of fuels. On the other hand, YSZ extends reaction zone in anode by providing ionic conduction path. During sintering, YSZ also prevents Ni from agglomerating. Ni-based cermets and Ni-YSZ meet most requirements for anode material used for SOFC. These include high ionic and electronic conductivity, stable in reducing environment, and at high operating temperatures, good chemical and thermal compatibility with YSZ electrolyte and low cost. However, Ni-based materials have poor redox stability and sulfur tolerance. Furthermore, Ni promotes carbon formation from hydrocarbon fuel whereas carbon formation does not take place when Cu is used as replacement. Decreasing the operating temperature of the cell indicates that materials having mismatch in CTE could be used without affecting the mechanical integrity of the anode during temperature transients.

With the growing demand for powerful and green energy storage systems, much research endeavor has been devoted to develop high-performance electrode materials for lithium ion batteries (LIBs), among which, TiO2 is an appreciable candidate for anode material due to its superior properties like cycling stability, low cost, abundance in nature and non-pollution. In comparison with carbon-based electrodes, the formation of massy SEI(solid electrolyte interphase) layers on the anode can be alleviated effectively as TiO2 has a relatively higher lithium insertion-extraction voltage (~1.7 V vs Li+/Li) when compared with the formation potential of SEI film, and thereby can effectually enhance the safety of batteries. Within the common four polymorphs of TiO2 which are anatase, rutile, brookite, and TiO2B, anatase is generally considered to be the most electrochemically active phase and thus it has been investigated for a long time in the broadest way. Furthermore, during the Li insertion-extraction process for anatase TiO2, there is a tiny volume change of less than 4% in the crystal structure, contributing to its excellent structural stability and cycle longevity. Additionally, it has a relatively large theoretical specific capacity which can reach 335 mAh g-1 when one lithium migrates from per formula unit of TiO2. Nevertheless, the practical limit for lithium ions into/from bulk anatase is only 0.5 lithium per TiO2 unit, corresponding to a specific capacity of 167.5 mAh g-1 due to the diffusion limitation in the solid phase. From another perspective, the application of TiO2 as anode materials is restricted by its intrinsic poor electronic conductivity which has negative influence on its high-rate performances.

In order to improve the specific capacity of TiO2 anode at high-rate current densities, numerous strategies have been put into practice like minishing the TiO2 particle down to nanosize, doping with alien atoms and cooperating with high conductive agents. A variety of nanosized TiO2 materials have been constructed in order to increase the contact area between the electrode and electrolyte and reduce the diffusion length of Li ion and electron transport. Even so, the whole electrochemical performances of TiO2 are still not satisfactory due to its very low electronic conductivity of 10-14 S/cm. It has been demonstrated that incorporating with carbon materials on the surface of active particles is one of the most promising and effective solutions to improve the electronic conductivity of solid particles. To combine the merits of the excellent conductivity and the decrease of ion migration distance, conductive carbon can be deposited onto the TiO2 nanostructures either by adding a carbon precursor during the synthesis or by further coating carbon to the as-prepared materials. The former strategy is more efficient and appealing considering its simplified and lessened procedure and better homogeneous coating effects. However, these carbon-coating process in most cases often needs two or more steps in order to obtain the well-coated particles, which is relatively complicated and time-consuming. Therefore, it is still desirable to develop a cost-effective, time-saving and scalable route to prepare carbon-coated TiO2 for large-scale application with high electrochemical performances.

The excellent electrochemical performances of CTON could be ascribed to two main factors. Firstly, the superiority of nanosized particle for electrode has played the predominant role in the electrochemical properties. It has been investigated that during the charge/discharge process, the effective diffusion length for Li+ ion is 24-240 nm at the rate of 1 C, and 3.2-32 nm at 60 C. Hence, larger capacity could be obtained at high-rate current if the particle size of the electrode material can be decreased smaller than the above lengths. In this study, the particle size of the well-crystallined CTON has been decreased to as small as 20-30 nm, which can significantly shorten the Li ion transportation length especially in the high rate, resulting in enhanced the rate performances of this electrode material. Also, the nanostructure could provide sufficient electrode-electrolyte contact area for pseudocapacity from the lithium storage reaction. Secondly, the coated carbon has improved the electronic conductivity of TiO2 and lowered the energy barrier for lithium ion transport, which can prompt the high-rate performances. On the other hand, more Li+ ions could be facilitated to be storaged in accessible interphase sites of TiO2 and coated carbon. The interfacial storage machanism would be especially important in nanosized materials due to the high fractions of the interfacial regions.

Rietveld refinements based on XRD data were performed using the GSAS suite of programs . Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) studies were performed using a MERLIN machine from Zeiss. In this study, we synthesized N-GQDs by carbonizing hemp fibers at 180°C for 1 h to remove surface lignin, followed by hydrothermal reaction in the presence of sulfuric acid, hydrogen peroxide, and ethylenediamine ( a). Hemp fiber was chosen due to its abundant availability, low cost, high yield and sustainable nature. Ethylenediamine was added to incorporate nitrogen heteroatoms in GQDs. In addition, ethylenediamine rendered the reaction mixture basic nature and facilitated the formation of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals from hydrogen peroxide. The free radicals cleaved the bonds at the defective sites of the carbonized hemp fibers, resulting in a high yield (55 %) of N-GQDs, which were homogeneously dispersed in water. The ultraviolet-visible absorption spectrum of N-GQDs showed a sharp peak in the wavelength range of 270-300 nm with a tail extending to 390 nm, which is a characteristic band indicating the polyaromatic structure and n-p* transitions of graphene . Upon exposure to 365 nm light, N-GQDs emitted blue light ( b). This was attributed to the combined effects of quantum confinement and blocking of the edge-site functional groups . The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of N-GQDs( b) revealed their uniform particle size distribution (<5 nm) and the lattice spacing of N-GQDs(~0.35 nm) corresponds to the (0 0 2) plane of graphite.

The effects of temperature on the electrochemical behavior of \beta- Li x V2O5 bronze as cathode in Li-ion batteries have been explored by galvanostatic charge/discharge and EIS analysis. Superior cycle life with 82.3 %, 79.5 %, 88.6% capacity retention were observed under 0 °C, -20°C and -40 °C, respectively, in comparison with that of 55.0% at 25 °C. The lithiation kinetic properties have been investigated by EIS experiments, and it is shown that both of the charge-transfer and solid-state lithium diffusion activation energy are approximately identical at different SOC and SOD. Thus, the dominant limitation factors of the low temperature performance of \beta- LixV2O5 bronze are the slow charge-transfer kinetics as well as the solid-state Li+ diffusion within Li x V2O5 particles. More effective approaches, such as surface modification, particle size minimization, conductive phase incorporation, should be employed to enhance the low temperature performance of this material.

Ion intercalation into graphite can be divided into 4 steps -a) diffusion of solvated ions towards the host electrode through the electrolyte, b) desolvation of ions, c) crossing electrode-electrolyte interphase (EEI) barrier, and d) diffusion of desolvated ions inside the graphite lattice . Energetics of anion intercalation differ from cations. Firstly, liquid state diffusion has a negligible barrier among all steps. Secondly, desolvation and EEI crossing are termed together as interfacial charge transfer, among which desolvation is the most energy-consuming process for cation intercalation (50-70 kJ mol^-1 for Li+) . Bulky anions undergo weaker solvation, and the kinetics of shedding smaller solvation sheath is faster. That is why the activation energy of interfacial anion transfer is only 10-30 kJ mol^-1 . Thirdly, Li+ diffusivity into graphite (D c L i + = 10^-9 -10^-7 cm^2 s^-1) is much faster than anions ( PF6 - = 10-12 -10-13 cm2 S-1) . Therefore, interfacial charge transfer possesses the highest activation energy barrier for cation transfer, whereas solid-state mass transfer is the rate-limiting step for anion storage. Thicker electrodes bring additional challenges by reducing the utilization of active material. Inadequate electrolyte transport, a tortuous path for electronic and ionic percolation, weakening of mechanical integrity, etc., create more hindrances . Hence, optimization 4 is dedicated to study anion storage performance at extremely high current rates with thicker electrodes and to find optimum loading for the best power yield. Electrochemical performances of HfSiC2 with 5, 10, 15 mg cm-2 loading are compared at low and high current rates.

Current years has witnessed some progresses in the development of cathode materials for aqueous ZIBs, which can be mainly divided into four families (manganese-based oxides, vanadium-based oxides, Prussian blue analogues and organic compounds) [ ]. Vanadium-based oxides exhibit high capacity and good cycling stability, but they are high toxicity and the operation voltage is too low (around 0.75 V) . Prussian blue analogues possess high working voltages, long cycle life and good rate capability, but they suffer from inferior capacity of less than 70 mA h g-1 . Organic compounds are also explored to be attractive cathodes for aqueous ZIBs in recent years, but the energy density and cycling stability are far from satisfactory [ ]. By contrast, manganese-based oxides possess high theoretical capacity, moderate operation voltage, abundant resources and environmental friendliness, which holds great promise as prospective host materials for aqueous ZIBs . So far, a variety of manganese-based oxides including MnO, MnO2, Mn2O3, Mn3O4, ZnMn2O4, MgMn2O4, ect. have been reported. Unfortunately, manganese-based oxides severely suffer from the inherent poor electronic conductivity, sluggish reaction kinetics, huge volume expansion and dissolution of manganese species in electrolyte upon cycling, resulting in unsatisfactory rate capability and rapid capacity degeneration.

During the de-intercalation of lithium, the inner part of the particle with higher will exert a tensile stress on the outer part while the outer part will exert a compressive stress on the inner part of the particle. On the contrary, during intercalation, the inner part of the particle exerts a compressive force on the surface of the particle and the outer part a tensile stress on the core of the particle. The existence of the SEI layer will result in an additional compressive force in the whole particle, shifting the stress towards more negative values in both cases. However, due to the low stiffness in the SEI layer, the stresses in the active material will be barely modified. Therefore, the modification of the stress values in the active material will strongly depend on the stiffness of the SEI layer. Larger moduli will lead to larger compressive forces acting on the particle. Furthermore, the growth of the SEI layer would lead to material constriction in the electrode exerting an additional outer compressive force.

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have been commercialized for a long time and pursued in many fields such as portable electronics and electric vehicles . Limited by the low energy density, LIBs are far from meeting the growing market demands. Lithium-sulfur batteries (LSBs) with high theoretical specific capacity (~1675 mA h g-1) and energy density (~2600 W h kg-1) are regarded as promising alternatives to LIBs . However, the development of LSBs has been hindered by a series of challenges of the sulfur cathode that has a serious volume expansion during cycling, the insulation of both sulfur and polysulfides, and the shuttling effect of soluble long-chain lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) . These detrimental issues lead to poor rate capability, rapid capacity decay, and non-negligible corrosion of the lithium anode.

There are other two challenges facing the LSBs: (1) The unstable structure of LSBs which is mainly caused by the inferior anchoring ability of soluble polysulfides on the cathodic side and (2) the violent corrosion and lithium-dendrite formation that happen on the anodic side. The both challenges will result in inevitable performance degradation and serious safety issues . Pioneering studies have demonstrated that introducing functional interlayers in the cells can alleviate the two problems . On the one hand, the interlayers can effectively block and convert the polysulfides that are dissolved in the electrolyte, thus improving the utilization of sulfur and enhancing the capacity and cycling performance of LSBs. On the other hand, the interlayers can act as a hinder to inhibit the migration of polysulfides so that the anodic corrosion can be alleviated and the lithium-dendrite formation can be suppressed by the interlayers through reducing the uneven lithium deposition . To achieve the outstanding functions mentioned above, the interlayer is required excellent electrolyte wettability for rapid Li+ transfer, strong physical/chemical adsorption of polysulfides, and high catalytic activity to accelerate the conversion of LiPSs. The capability of rapid LiPSs anchoring-conversion is also important, which can avoid the LiPSs accumulation to damage the interlayer, prevent the low sulfur utilization caused by the polysulfides shuttling, and ensure the structural stability of lithium anode . Among the studied materials, metal oxide/sulfide heterostructures with strong chemisorption, unique conductive heterointerface, and rapid LiPSs catalytic conversion, have been reported as ideal materials for functional interlayers . However, intensive efforts have been reported to improve the defects of cathode or anode through modifying cathode materials or introducing interlayers, but few systematic designs have simultaneously alleviated all the above issues in dual-side electrodes.

Herein, we demonstrated a novel strategy to synchronously tackle the aforementioned problems on cathode and anode of LSBs via the synergetic of the efficient catalytic host cathode and light multifunctional interlayer. Both the sulfur host and the multifunctional interlayer based on an interconnected carbonized bacterial cellulose network (CBC) are co-applied to deliver their specifial functions in LSBs. The low-cost CBC with intrinsic 3 D interconnected porous network structure can accommodate the tremendous volume expansion of transformed sulfur, offer physical adsorption to suppress the shuttling effect, and accelerate the Li+ diffusivity during cycling . A hierarchical structure of SnO2-SnS2 heterostructures coated on the nanofibers of the CBC network coordinating high-conductivity carbon nanofibers (ht-CNFs) was fabricated as the multifunctional interlayer (CBC/SOSC). CBC/SOSC can rapidly capture soluble LiPSs via the strong adsorption and accelerate the catalytic conversion, realizing the enhanced regulation of LiPSs from capture to conversion. In addition, the significance of CBC/SOSC for safety issues arising on the anodic side was highlighted. CBC/SOSC can promote the uniform Li deposition, which suppressed the lithium-dendrite formation and improved the stability of SEI formation. It has been proved that the Na2WO4 can be used as an effective electrolyte additive to improve the high-temperature performance of Ni-MH cells with either KOH electrolyte or NaOH electrolyte. It is found that by adding (1.0 wt. %) Na2WO4, the performance of nickel electrodes is significantly improved in both NaOH and KOH electrolytes at 70 °C. CV tests indicate that the charge acceptance of Ni-MH cell can be improved due to the high overvoltage for oxygen evolution. The steady-state polarization measurements show that the use of Na2WO4 additive is beneficial to the controlling of OER in KOH electrolyte. This performance improvement is also ascribed to the lower charge-transfer resistance, as indicated by EIS. The mechanism of the enhanced performance of Ni-MH cells has been investigated. Based on the results of XRD and SEM, it can be concluded that the improved performance can be attributed to the deposition of WO3·2 H2O solid film on the surface of nickel electrode, which plays an important role to the increase in oxygen evolution overvoltage, the slow-down of oxygen evolution and the decrease in charge-transfer resistance. Therefore, Na2WO4 is an effective electrolyte additive to improve the high-temperature performance of nickel hydroxide cathode for Ni-MH batteries.

The modified separators were assembled in the cells, as well as the conventional PP separators for comparison. 1 M LiPF6-ethylene carbonate/diethyl carbonate was employed as the electrolyte. Full-cells were assembled by coupling the graphite anodes with LiFePO4 cathodes in the weight ratio of 1:2.2. In pursuit of alternatives to LIBs, other energy carriers (Na and K) of the same alkali series have been the focus of attention during the past years. Na and K are not only abundantly available but also distribute all around the world . Moreover, PIBs and sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) share the same working principle as their counterpart of LIBs, which implies the feasibility to apply the research concepts and methodologies in LIBs to PIBs and SIBs. When further comparing these two emerging batteries, PIBs even demonstrate electrochemical superiority in some aspects  . For instance, K+ generally has the smallest desolvation energy in PC and the highest ionic conductivity in EC/EDC-based electrolytes as compared to Na+ and Li+, which is beneficial to achieve facile insertion and diffusion of ion in batteries . In addition, different from Na+, K+ can be intercalated into the well-known commercial graphite anode at room temperature with reversible capacities in excess of 200 mAh/g; the intercalation voltage (~0.2 V vs . K/K+) is low and comparable to that of Li+ intercalation, which gives rise to high voltage of graphite-based PIBs . With the aforementioned merits, PIBs have manifested even comparable comprehensive performance to LIBs in some cases. On the other hand, the low standard electrochemical potential of K/K+ (lower than that of Na/Na+ and comparable to that of Li/Li+) has stimulated the development of potassium metal batteries, which share the same cathode materials to PIBs; thus the achievements in potassium metal batteries also facilitate the PIBs design .

Placing the sampling event att 1 with respect to the reference level at t 0 determines the total capacitance with the contribution of all relaxation processes with the time constants smaller than t 1: C = C(0) + C( t 1) ( b). The sampling time corresponds approximately to the reciprocal value of frequency used at the standard capacitance measurements by a harmonic signal. DLTS technique detects capacitance or charge relaxations due to the charge emission from the defect states or due to the dielectric polarization ( c). The basic idea consists of the rate window concept, i.e. transient capacitance or charge is processed by the correlation function Q = Q( t 1) -1.5 Q(2 t 1) + 0.5 Q(4 t 1) . This function generates a DLTS peak in the case when a transient signal has a time constant comparable with the sampling timet 1. Therefore the contribution to the total capacitance in time domain can be directly correlated to the relaxation observed with the DLTS. Isothermal DLTS is a modification of original technique where, instead a fixed rate window and sweeping temperature, the relaxation processes are investigated at fixed temperature and rate window is swept.

The electrochemical properties of pristine SiO, prelithiated SiO(L67), and Si/TiSi2/Li2SiO3(LT10, LT25, and LT50) were investigated by preparing an electrode slurry of each sample. The slurries were prepared by hand-mixing using agate mortar with 80 wt.% active materials, 10 wt.% conductive agent (Super-P), and 10 wt.% binder (commercial vendor) dissolved in deionized water. The slurries were coated on a copper foil using a Baker film applicator (YBA-3, Yoshimitsu). Coated electrode slurries were then dried in a convection oven at 80  for 1 h followed by a pressing process under 200 kg cm-2 to achieve a uniform electrode thickness of 50 µm. Pressed electrodes were dried in a vacuum at 100  for 2 h to remove residual moisture. Coin-type half cells (CR2032, Wellcos Co.) were assembled in an argon-filled glove box. The half cells were assembled with prepared electrodes, lithium metal foils (200 \mum, Honjo metal) used as a counter electrode, a polyethylene separator (Celgard 2400 membrane), and an electrolyte of 1.0 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate/ethyl methyl carbonate/diethyl carbonate (EC/EMC/DEC; 2:2:5, v/v/v; Panax Etec Co., Ltd.) with 10 wt.% of additional fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). Charge and discharge measurements of the coin-type half cells were performed using a battery cycle system (CTS-LAB, BaSyTec). The half cells of pristine SiO, prelithiated SiO, and Si/TiSi2/Li2SiO3 electrodes were galvanostatically discharged under a constant current-constant voltage (CC-CV) mode and charged under CC mode, with a voltage window between 0.01 and 1.5 V( vs. Li/Li+) at a current density of 50 mA g-1 for the initial three formation cycles and 500 mA g-1 for the subsequent 500 cycles. The Si/TiSi2/Li2SiO3 composite demonstrated a high initial coulombic efficiency of 89% and a reversible capacity of 1500 mAh/g after 100 cycles. The electrochemical impedance changes of pristine SiO, prelithiated SiO(L67), and Si/TiSi2/Li2SiO3(LT25) electrodes during cycling were monitored using impedance-analyzing potentiostat (VSP-300, BioLogic) over the frequency range of 1 MHz-10 mHz with an amplitude of 5 mV.

Generally, the degradation pattern of a battery consists of complex electrochemical reactions. For example, two common degradation modes are the loss of lithium inventory consumed by battery-side reactions and the loss of active material . The state-of-health (SOH) is the ratio of the current maximum discharge capacity to the initial capacity, which has been widely applied to evaluate battery performance [ ]. LIBs capacity degradation is complex and non-linear, which brings difficulties in accurately estimating SOH. Accurate capacity and SOH estimations contribute to the reliable usage of lithium batteries and avoid catastrophic implications. A typical commercial LIB might start with a specific capacity of 180 mAh g-1 and a cycle life of 1000-2000 cycles before significant degradation.

The increasing ubiquity of electric vehicles and intelligent electronic equipment has motivated extensive research on high-energy-density power systems beyond current lithium Li ion batteries (LIBs). Among the numerous anode electrodes for energy devices, Li metal with the highest theoretical capacity (3,860 mAh g-1) and lowest reduction potential (-3.04 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode), has been considered the ultimate candidate for the anode . However, due to the intrinsic active nature of Li metal, the utility of the consummate Li metal anodes still confronts many challenges. First, the distribution of Li+ at the electrolyte/anode interface is not uniform during the charge/discharge processes due to the local electric field effect, then the inhomogeneous Li stripping/depositing behaviors tend to generate detrimental dendrites and dead Li, which would cause an internal short circuit in the batteries . Second, the repeated stripping/plating processes may result in the instability and accumulation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Subsequently, the active Li and electrolyte continue to be depleted, and the diffusion of Li+ from the uneven SEI layer is limited . In addition, the pure commercial Li foils present poor mechanical properties and serious excess capacity, lead to lower energy density. Consequently, these infamous matters compel the Li metal battery with short life time and unsafety problems.

Many strategies have been reported to effectively restrain the Li dendrites and stabilize the SEI layer for stable Li metal battery, such as constructing a three-dimensional (3 D) host structure , engineering a stable artificial interfacial layer , functional separators and exploiting electrolyte additives to strengthen the electrostatic shield and optimize the SEI structure . Nevertheless, these solutions mainly focused on homogenizing the plating/stripping behaviors of Li+ on the electrode surface and eliminating the dendritic formation. Whereas the issues of Li+ concentration and distribution pattern at the electrolyte/anode interface were easily ignored. According to the Sand's model, the Li+ diffusivity effectively influences the depositing behaviour . Accompanying repeated stripping/deposition processes, the Li+ concentration would be decreased, and the distribution would be more vulnerable to unevenness, especially at high current densities with severe concentration polarization at the subsurface . This situations would increase the unordered ionic flux near the surface of electrode, which may promote drastic growth of Li dendrites . Therefore, maintaining an adequate concentration and high transport of Li+ is especially significant for reducing the concentration polarization, and thus resolving the diffusion-and advection-limited ionic transport in the bulk electrolyte, particularly at high cycling rates. The distribution patterns of the electrolyte are adversely affected by the electric field of the host. In addition, the reported 3D host materials generally cannot achieve quantitative Li loading to lower the areal Li ratio of negative and positive electrodes (N/P). Therefore, the excess Li reduces the energy density, and also may cause safety issues . Currently, constructing an ultrathin matrix to guide the quantitative capacity of Li anodes and induce the controllable Li+ electrochemical behaviors has not been proposed, especially from the viewpoint of the designated chemical structure and at the level of the electrolyte/anode interface.

Lithiation kinetics modulates stress generation and fracture . Previous studies revealed several features in lithiation shared by crystalline Si( c -Si) and Ge( c -Ge). Owing to the much higher surface diffusivity than the bulk in Si and Ge, Li quickly covers the surface of the nanostructures, and then flows inward, forming a core-shell structure with lithiated amorphous outer shell and unlithiated crystalline inner core . As lithiation proceeds, the shell thickens and the core shrinks. The amorphous-crystalline interface (ACI) separating the shell and the core was revealed to be atomically sharp , with a width of only ~1 nm . Across the interface, the Li concentration drops abruptly from Li3.75M(M=Si or Ge) to c -M. The amorphous region undergoes very large volume expansion (~300% for c -Si and ~260% for c -Ge) due to Li insertion. Large incompatible strain and stress are generated at the reaction front.

A core component of an ASSLIB is the solid electrolyte (SE), which controls the movement of ions and determines the performance of the ASSLIB. Among the various types of SEs, sulfide SEs are good candidates owing to their high ionic conductivity and deformability . Many studies have been devoted to the research and development of novel sulfide SEs. Recently, sulfide SEs with lithium-ion conductivities higher than that of the liquid electrolyte have been developed . However, ASSLIBs with higher performance cannot be realized solely by a higher SE ionic conductivity. The design and fabrication of a composite electrode, which is composed of an AM, SE, and an electron conductive additive (if necessary), are also essential. For high-performance ASSLIBs, a well-designed electrode with a large contact area between AMs and SEs, as well as well-percolated electron/ion transport pathways, is essential. However, both AMs and SEs are mostly in the form of fine cohesive particles (ca. < 10 µm), making it difficult to fabricate composite electrodes with such a desired structure without any powder preprocessing. Therefore, to overcome this challenge, it is necessary to develop a powder processing technology that produces composite particles suitable for the ASSLIB composite electrode.

Inspired by the chemical nature of electrostatic effect based Li host that enables improved mass transport , we proposed a interface-chemistry engineering to regulate the Li+ behavior through a partially reduced graphene oxide film (PrGO) with electronegative effect. On the one hand, the prepared PrGO with adjustable oxygen content is capable of realizing a quantitative Li capacity to obtain an ultrathin electrode based on PrGO@Li, which could vastly reduce the Li dosage. Furthermore, the optimized PrGO@Li electrode with manageable electronegativity can cause an electrostatic force and have a strong affinity for Li+, and the local Li+ concentration can be increased, and homogeneously distributed at the electrolyte/anode interface. Then a LiF-rich component would be contemporaneously formed in the SEI layer, and resulting in a lower interface energy, a stabler structure and higher ionic conductivity for Li+. The uniform SEI structure and strong electronegativity of oxygen groups suggest an uniform Li nucleation and lateral growth, resulting in a densely packed Li morphology without dendritic or dead Li. Ultimately, the PrGO@Li electrode shows an extremely low overpotential (7 mV) during Li stripping/plating process with uniform nucleation in a symmetric cell for a long cycling. When the anode is configured in the PrGO@Li//LiFePO4 full battery, the assembled device exhibits outstanding storage characteristics with a raised initial capacity, a high rate capacity and stable cycle life. In addition, benefiting from the flexibility of the PrGO film host, the pouch battery can regularly operate even with multiple bendings. This host is also adapted to sulfur S loading as a cathode for Li/S batteries with excellent electrochemical performance. In this research, we designed and optimized an electronegative PrGO film as ideal Li host, and demonstrated the effect of oxygen functional groups on the Li+ electrochemical behaviors by experimental and computational analyses. These PrGO films with tunable oxygen contents and strong electronegativity could absorb molten metallic Li to form an ultrathin PrGO@Li film with high strength and controllable areal capacity. The oxygen groups with low binding energy played a more important role than the porosity and conductivity on the infiltration of Li. The optimized electrode (PrGO@Li-400) with appropriate interfacial characterization could induce an increase in the Li+ concentration on the surface and maintain a uniform distribution, thus simultaneously forming a thin, uniform and stable SEI layer. The formed SEI layer was demonstrated to have rich LiF components with a high ionic conductivity of Li+. The uniform SEI structure and strong electronegativity of oxygen groups promoted uniform Li nucleation and lateral growth, resulting in a densely packed Li morphology without dendritic or dead Li. The optimized electrode achieved a high reversibility of Li plating/stripping behaviors with a lower overpotential at 20 mA cm-2 and 10 mAh cm-2 over 2000 h based on a symmetric cell. Further the assembled full batteries (coin and pouch) based on PrGO@Li film anodes without superfluous metallic Li showed excellent flexible storage characteristics as well. This interface-chemistry strategy provides a new insight into the fundamental understanding of the effect of the host molecular structure on the Li+ behaviors, high utilization rate and rational design of anodes for high-performance Li-based batteries.

It is worth remembering that the battery self-consumption due to the heater actions was not considered in the model. This simplification is licit because the exothermic cell reactions themselves guarantee the battery operating temperature in steady state operations. The heaters are involved when the battery temperature drops below 260 °C, therefore it implies a little heater power consumption, which can be neglected. Overall, although the cells have 100% coulombic efficiency, and therefore, have no self-discharge , the base operating temperature of 260 °C requires that even in a very well insulated battery box utilizing evacuated thermal insulation, some heat loss is unavoidable. A 20 kWh battery would have a heat loss of around 80 W and this can be thought of as self-discharge. It is not possible to classify this as a percentage of capacity since it depends upon the operating cycle but it varies from 10% per day if the battery is not used at all (exhibiting a natural cooling of around 3 °C/h ) to zero for an intensively used battery in which the temperature never falls to 260 °C. In order to increase the model accuracy and to consider the battery stand-by mode or a very low current charge or discharge for a short time, the heaters influence should be taken into account. The pouch cell furthermore exhibits a capacity of 26 mAh with no observed degradation after 250 cycles, demonstrating immense potential for practical applications. Among various rechargeable cells, lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries have gained critical importance due to their higher energy density, higher operating voltage, lower self-discharge and lower maintenance requirement . Therefore, increasing the charge and energy density of Li-ion batteries has been the centerpiece of many studies in the past. It has been shown that noticeable increase in the charge capacity is achievable through replacing the conventional carbonaceous anodes with high-capacity Li-alloy (Li+ M; M = Sn, Si, Ge, Al) anodes . To alleviate the mechanical stresses and avoid the associated mechanical failure modes, many recent studies have focused on nano-scale electrodes in the form of particles , wires  and films . Although nano-structured electrodes generally exhibit improved mechanical performance as compared to their bulk counterparts, recent theoretical as well as experimental studies reveal that mechanical failure can still take place in nano-electrodes .

While the high voltage LiCoPO4 cathode delivers an acceptable capacity and rate performance without the need of excessive conductive carbon (as is done for a LiMnPO4 cathode), LiCoPO4 has been reported to have a fast fade in capacity upon electrochemical cycling which limits its application. Numerous reports on the origin of the poor cycling stability of LiCoPO4 indicate that the fast capacity fading in LiPF6 containing electrolyte solutions is believed to be due to the nucleophilic attack of the HF(always) present in these electrolyte on the P atoms of the olivine compound in the delithiated state resulting in the formation of soluble PO3F2-, PO2F2-, POF3 and H2O. The H2O produced then reacts with PF6-, POF3 and PO2F2- to produce more HF [ ]. Therefore, to prevent CoPO4 dissolution during cycling, HF should ideally be eliminated -which is a challenging task. Various strategies have been tested to stabilize the cycling performance including the use of an HF scavenging separator, protective coating, and doping to induce SEI(solid electrolyte interphase) layer formation using electrolyte additives [ ]. Using the latter approach, Fe-substituted LiCoPO4 exhibited an improved cycling stability due to the stabilization of the structure in the delithiated state [ ]. However, a lower specific capacity was achieved when Fe was used as a dopant. Recently, various electrolyte additives have also improved the cycling performance. An improved capacity retention was observed when LiCoPO4 was cycled with an electrolyte containing either tris (hexafluoroisopropyl) phosphate (HFiP) or trimethylboroxine (TMB) . Additionally, the use of alternative separators such as glassy paper or quartz has increased the cycling stability relative to the conventional polyethylene (PE)/polypropylene (PP) separators due to the presence of silica, which is known to be a HF scavenger.

Metallic Li has been considered as the most promising anode material to satisfy the increasing demand of energy density due to its ultra-high specific capacity (3860 mAh g-1, vs. 372 mAh g-1 of graphite) and the lowest reduction potential (-3.04 V vs standard hydrogen electrode) . However, the Li dendrite arising from uneven Li plating and the low coulombic efficiency due to the highly reactive nature of Li within electrolytes preclude the commercial application of rechargeable lithium metal batteries (LMBs) . Besides, the continuous electrolyte oxidation on the catalytic high-voltage cathodes also compromises the LMBs cycle life for high-voltage operation due to poor anodic stability of conventional electrolytes . The key to achieving highly reversible LMBs is to construct robust and stable interphase films (SEI/cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI)), which present high and uniform Li+ conductivity, high mechanical strength, as well as the thermodynamic stability to passivate both Li anodes and aggressive cathodes. To achieve these goals, LiF has been proposed and demonstrated as one of the optimal SEI/CEI components, due to the advantages of low solubility , high Young's modulus, wide band gap (effectively prevents electron tunneling) , and high interface energy (accommodates the large volume expansion of Li anodes and cathodes).

Li-ion batteries or lithium batteries (LIBs) are playing key roles as power sources in various areas, such as consumer electronics and electric vehicles . All-solid-state LIBs using solid-state Li-ion conductors as electrolytes are regarded as power devices with high energy density and safe, and can be paired with both high-voltage cathode and high-capacity Li metal anodes (3860 mAh g-1) . The solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) can be divided into two major categories: inorganic solid electrolytes (e.g., sulfides and oxides) and polymer electrolytes (e.g., polyethyleneoxide (PEO)). The inorganic SSEs may have high ionic conductivity (10-4 to 10-2 S cm-1), mechanical rigidity and non-flammability . However, the brittleness and poor interface contact with electrodes limit the application of inorganic SSEs. Polymer electrolytes have the merit of flexibility and processability, but their low intrinsic Li-ion conductivity (10-8 to 10-6 S cm-1) at ambient temperature and insufficient mechanical strength could not meet the application challenge . Inorganic/organic composite solid electrolytes (CSEs) composed of inorganic Li-ion conductors and polymer electrolytes possess the advantages of high conductivity and mechanical strength . The high mechanical strength can inhibit dendrite penetration, while the introduction of electrolyte particles can improve the ionic conductivity of composite solid electrolytes (CSEs) . The flexibility of organic components can ensure the manufacturability of CSE and effective contact with electrode materials . The CSEs provide the opportunity for fabricating high packing efficiency, flexible and safe batteries.

The pursuit of green energy in electrochemical energy storage devices is continually propelled by pivotal criteria such as high energy density, cost-effectiveness, long cycle life, abundance, safety, and ease of manufacturing . In recent years, Lithium-sulfur batteries (LSBs) have emerged as the next-generation energy storage solution owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density and capacity, reaching up to 1675 mAh g-1 . With the potential to produce up to 2600 Wh kg-1, LSBs significantly outmatch commercial Li-ion batteries, which typically yield less than 250 Wh kg-1 . Despite these promising attributes, the commercialization of LSBs encounters obstacles due to intrinsic issues like low active material utilization, high solubility of lithium polysulfides (LiPS), and subpar cycling performance and rate capability [ ]. The limited utilization of active materials stems from sulfur's insulating nature, hindering efficient electron/ion transfer during electrochemical reactions . Additionally, LSBs suffer from the negative effects of LiPS intermediate dissolution during discharge, inducing a shuttle effect between the anode and cathode . This phenomenon results in the loss of active material, leading to rapid capacity decay and contamination of metallic lithium anode. To address these challenges and advance the feasibility of LSBs, it is imperative to enhance sulfur loading on the cathode while effectively managing the retention or re-utilization of soluble LiPSs within the cathode region.

Two-dimensional layered inorganic compounds, called MXenes (Mn+1XnTx, n = 1, 2, 3), where M is transition metal (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, etc.), X is N and/or C, Tx is surface group (-F, =O, -OH, etc.), have been deemed as the popular materials in electrochemical field owing to favourable electronic conductivity, preeminent hydrophilicity, intercalated structure, high surface area and abundant active sites. For example, Simon's group prepared MXenes through molten salt etching using metal chlorides. Gu and his co-workers successfully removed the Al layer from MAX phase in NaOH-assisted hydrothermal process. Hao's group applied thermal-assisted electrochemical etching method to obtain MXenes. The electronegativity and controllable interlayer structure are favorable to the adsorption and storage of metal ions such as Li+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ and other ions, thus MXenes are convenient to be used as moderate precursors to synthesize other materials. Among these metal ions, the radius of hydrated Mg2+ (4.28 Å) is larger than that of other metal ions (e.g., 3.82 Å for Li+, 3.58 Å for Na+, 3.31 Å for K+, 4.12 Å for Ca2+). From another point of view, Na-ion is larger in size (1.02 Å) than Li-ion (0.76 Å), which affects structural properties of the electrodes , the ion intercalation/de-intercalation and, indirectly, the charge compensation mechanisms . For 3D current collectors, the pore size, pore volume, and specific surface area are essential parameters affecting the metal plating/stripping. The pore volume and size determine the amounts of deposited metals that can be accommodated. The specific surface area is pivotal for sufficient electric contact between current collectors and active metals, and the high surface area of 3D current collectors promotes favorable electrolyte contact and charge transfer kinetics. As a result, a dendrite-free cycling behavior is realized during the cycling processes. For example, Luo and co-workers proposed a porous Al current collector as a deposition framework to inhibit Na dendrites. Obviously, NG/Si@NC exhibits greatly improved cycle life over G/Si@C and G/Si. Note that the reversible capacity of G/Si quickly fades to 240 mAh g-1 after 100 cycles with a low retention of 13 %. The poor cycling performance can be ascribed to the fact that graphene is unable to restrain the volume expansion of SiNPs, and that the aggregated and un-enwrapped SiNPs exposed on graphene experience continuous formation of unstable SEI. After coating with a carbon layer onto SiNPs, the cyclability of G/Si@C shows a significant improvement, retaining at 603 mAh g-1 after 100 cycles with a 64% retention, which is mainly due to the double protection from the carbon layer on the surface of SiNPs and graphene, which can synergistically buffer the volume variation and enhance the conductivity . In sharp contrast, NG/Si@NC electrode exhibits an initial reversible capacity of 1142 mAh g-1 and remains at 938 mAh g-1 after 100 cycles with an 82% retention. The greatly enhanced reversible capacity and cycling stability of NG/Si@NC over G/Si@C can be attributed to the following aspects. Firstly, N-doping can induce a large amount of topological defects on graphene nanosheets and carbon layer and form a disordered carbon structure, which can enhance Li storage properties . Secondly, the pyridinic N atoms in NG and NC can improve the reversible capacity of NG/Si@NC . Thirdly, NG can increase the wettability of NG/Si@NC toward organic electrolytes, and promote ion diffusion at the interface between the electrode and electrolyte, thus improving the electrochemical performance .

In summary, we have developed a novel inner coating method, which using 1 D CNTs as inner coating materials for the application of manganese dioxides with low electronic conductivity and high volume change for lithium-ion batteries. The 1 D conductive CNTs insert into the MnO2 microspheres and intertwine together to form a three-dimensional conductive and mechanical network, which not only improves conductivity but it also accommodates volume change in the active material. Several advantages can be obtained through the 3 D network: first, the 3 D conducting network enables both Li+ and e+ to migrate and reach every active particle; hence, achieving the full utilization of all active materials; second, the 3 D mechanical network can relieve the strain of active materials during lithiation/delithiation. The electrochemical tests have demonstrated that the synthesized inner coating of the MnO2@CNT can achieve extremely high Li-storage capacity (1097.3 mAh g-1), high rate capability and superior cycling stability. In view of its facile synthesis, efficient charge transportation, and the effect in maintaining the integrity of the electrode during the volume expansion/contraction, this method can also be applied to other high capacity electrode materials, and as a result, promoting the development of next-generation lithium-ion batteries.

The development of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) continued to improve in line with the expansion of high-energy storage requirements. To date, the most commonly used anode material in LIBs, being Graphite, has been unable to meet this demand due to its' low theoretical capacity of 372 mAh g-1. Transition metal oxide (TMO) although have some advantages such as the ultra-high theoretical specific capacity, low cost and abundant resources, but there are still issues and challenges, including the large volume expansion which degrades cycle life to less than 100 cycles in many cases, low lithium ion diffusivity (~10-16 cm2 s-1) and poor electronic conductivity (~10-7 S cm-1). These factors together have hindered TMO's wider application. In researching how to enhance TMO, a number of studies have focused on two aspects: The first potential modification method is to create nano-sized TMOs, which extends to nanoparticles, nanorods and nanofibers. The second is synthesizing carbon-containing composite materials using carbon nanotubes, graphene and amorphous carbon. The capacity of these carbon-based composites is relatively low, and the synthesis methods require complicated processes and longer reaction times.

Based on the analysis of detailed electrochemical behaviors and origination of irreversible capacity for iron oxalate, we summarize three distinct modified strategies to improve the reversible capacity and capacity retention. 1. Adulteration or coating carbonaceous substances such as reduced graphene oxide . Modification with high-electrical conductivity materials can improve the mobility of Li+ ions in channels and enhance the activity of electrochemical reactions within active materials. This method is extraordinarily effective to improve the reversible capacity in both the conversion reaction and capacitive effect processes. 2. Controllable synthesis for different morphologies and structural organization . The specific structure can offer more channels and shorten the pathways for Li+ ions diffusion and electron conduction to enhance the reactivity of electrochemical products. Moreover, the stabilized structure can also avoid the collapsing of particles and cracking caused by volume expansion, ensuring the formation of a stable SEI membrane on the surface of the particles. 3. Controlling the thickness of "organic” layer and inhibiting the interfacial reactions caused by the consumption of electrolyte can effectively decrease the irreversible capacity. Hence, we recognize that the design interface of electrodes and material particles is still a vital role for achieving high reversible capacity, excellent cycle life of 1000 cycles, and superior high-rate capability of transition-metal oxalates. To date, the most commonly used anode material in LIBs, being Graphite, has been unable to meet this demand due to its' low theoretical capacity (372 mAh g-1) . SOFCs(solid oxide fuel cells) are environmentally friendly power generation systems with high efficiency. The conventional SOFCs consist of cathode (LSM/YSZ), electrolyte (YSZ), and anode (NiO/YSZ), which are usually operated at above 900°C due to the low ionic conductivity of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) . However, it has been reported that high operating temperature leads to cell degradation, which reduces the life of the SOFC. To decrease the operating temperature, two approaches are studied; one is the reduction of the electrode thickness of the electrolyte as thin as few tens of micrometers, another is the application of alternative electrolyte materials such as La SrGa MgO3-d(LSGM) and Sm2O3 doped CeO2(SDC) . Therefore, new electrolyte materials with high ionic conductivity at lower operating temperature have been investigated. LaGaO3-based materials with perovskite structure have been kept attention on electrolyte systems with high ionic conductivity at below 800 °C . Strontium and magnesium-doped lanthanum gallate composition (LSGM, La0.8Sr0.2Ga0.8Mg0.2O3-d) is one of the candidate materials for intermediate temperature solid oxide fuel cells (IT-SOFCs) . However, it has also been reported that there are some difficulties on synthesizing LSGM material of single phase with high ionic conductivity and when LSGM material was applied as electrolyte layer of SOFC single cell, side reaction products were created such as LaNiO3 or La2NiO4 . They were formed at the interface of LSGM electrolyte and anode layer at high sintering temperature, resulting in the degradation of SOFC cell . Therefore, it is reported that design of electrolyte-support type is usually applied for the fabrication of LSGM-based SOFC cell, in which first of all, electrolyte support with thick electrode thickness of above 300 µm is prepared by sintering process. Among them, V-based layered oxides are considered as promising cathode candidates because the open frameworks provide numerous diffusion paths and storage space for Zn2+. However, the long-term cycle life of V-based layered oxides is unsatisfactory owing to the stability penalty induced by the aqueous system and large Zn2+ radius. To overcome these issues, tremendous efforts have been devoted over the past few years . Among them, interlayer engineering, i.e., pre-intercalating metal ions into layers, is an effective strategy to stabilize the layered frameworks . Various metal ions , such as Na+ , K+ , Mg2+ , and Ca2+ , have been pre-introduced into V-based layered oxides to enlarge the interlayer spacing and strengthen the structural stability, but with the increase of the mass of electrochemically inactive elements. Another common strategy is defect engineering, which could induce the electronic structure reconfiguration and accelerate charge transfer kinetics to boost the reversible Zn2+ storage . For instance, anionic vacancies, such as O and Se vacancies, have been induced to reduce the strong electrostatic interaction between oxides and Zn2+, reducing lattice strain due to Zn2+ insertion/extraction and accelerating Zn2+ diffusivity. Meanwhile, several reports have proposed the introduction of cationic vacancies to provide additional sites for Zn2+ storage to improve the capacity . However, only cationic or anionic defects have limit effects on enhancing the electrochemical performance . Therefore, coupling interlayer and defect engineering may offer a reliable opportunity to construct high capacity and stable V-based layered oxide cathodes for ZIBs.

The electrochemcial performance of the HVO@C cathode was investigated in a wide voltage window (1.5-4.0 V vs. Li/Li+). This wide range allows for observing various potential Li-ion intercalation/de-intercalation processes. As a result, the initial cycle, a, displayed a multi-step Li interaction, evident in two distinct redox peak pairs. The peaks at 2.70/3.15 V and 2.45/2.80 V, suggest separate redox mechanisms with significant potential differences of 450 mV and 350 mV, respectively. This indicates complex electrochemical behavior within the HVO@C structure. Interestingly, a small shoulder irreversibly appeared on the second reduction peak (2.45 V) during the second cycle. This suggests the presence of unreacted HVO@C from the first cycle, finally reacting with Li-ions, requiring more cycles for complete utilization. From the third cycle onward, a stable pair of peaks emerged at 2.75/3.15 V. This indicates the growth of a stable solid-electrolyte interface (SEI) and a reversible phase within the cathode, signifying improved electrode kinetics. Compared with a reported CV of V2O5-based cathodes, the CV curves exhibit a relatively large baseline separation between discharge and charge currents, suggesting a pseudocapacitive contribution to the overall capacity.  This can be ascribed to the presence of amorphous HVO@C, which allows for fast surface-based Li storage and contributes to improved rate capability. In general, the HVO@C cathode exhibits promising electrochemical performance with stable cycling behavior and a pseudocapacitive contribution. However, the multi-step redox processes and initial irreversibility require further investigation to optimize the material's full potential.
